analysis.one_liner: Bans new offshore oil and gas drilling leases off Florida's Gulf coast.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a House vote; it sat in committee until the 101st Congress ended in January 1991.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have barred the Interior Department from leasing federal offshore lands south of 26 degrees north latitude and east of 86 degrees west longitude — the waters off southwest Florida and the Keys — for oil and gas drilling, including any exploration or production approvals. It also directed Interior to write rules for buying back any existing leases in that area. The bill was introduced by a Florida Republican with 31 cosponsors from both parties, was referred to the Interior and Insular Affairs Committee, and never came out of it.
analysis.who_benefits: Residents and visitors of Florida's Gulf coast, whose beaches, fisheries, and tourism economy would be protected from oil spills and drilling infrastructure; Florida's fishing and tourism businesses, which depend on clean coastal waters.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Florida coastal communities and tourism businesses

how_it_helps.text: The bill prohibits the Interior Secretary from any preleasing or leasing activity — calls for information, tract selection, notices of sale, bids, or lease awards — for offshore submerged lands south of 26 degrees north latitude and east of 86 degrees west longitude, covering the eastern Gulf off southwest Florida [S3].
It also blocks approval of any exploration plan or development and production plan in the same area, so even previously identified tracts could not move toward drilling [S3].
It directs Interior to issue guidelines for the United States to buy back existing oil and gas leases in the protected zone, retiring drilling rights that were already sold [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas companies lose access to new federal drilling acreage off Florida, and existing leaseholders would look to a federal buyback rather than compensation through drilling; the Treasury forgoes lease sale revenue and would fund buybacks of existing leases.
analysis.who_pays_short: Oil companies and federal lease revenue

drawbacks.text: Buying back existing leases would require the federal government to pay leaseholders, and Section 2 provides no funding source for those payments — the cost would fall on taxpayers [S2] [S3].

The ban would remove a region from domestic oil and gas production, forgoing federal lease revenue and adding supply pressure at a time when the US imported a large share of its oil; oil and gas interests argued offshore areas like the eastern Gulf hold significant reserves.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The environmental and tourism stakes for Florida are large and the drilling risk is permanent once leases are issued, so the main cost — foregone lease revenue and buyback payments — is real but modest compared with a spill's damage. The buyback provision, without a funding mechanism, is the bill's weakest design feature.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the House Interior and Insular Affairs Committee, which referred it to a subcommittee and never reported it, so it died when the 101st Congress ended in January 1991.

narrative.text: Representative Andrew Ireland of Florida introduced the bill on July 20, 1989, joined by ten other Florida House members, including both Democrats and Republicans [S3].
The bill attracted 31 cosponsors — 20 Democrats and 11 Republicans — giving it bipartisan support concentrated in the Florida delegation [S4].
The House referred it to the Committee on Interior and Insular Affairs on the day of introduction; it was never reported out [S5].
On September 8, 1989, it went to the Subcommittee on Water, Power and Offshore Energy Resources, where it stayed for the rest of the Congress [S5].
The committee requested an executive comment from the Interior Department in September and held a field hearing in Key West in October 1989, but no further action followed [S5].
No floor vote ever occurred in the House or Senate, and the bill expired when the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991 [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and gas interests kept the eastern Gulf off Florida available for potential future leasing, and no taxpayer money was spent on lease buybacks; Florida's coastal areas gained no new legal protection from the bill's death, since existing policy still governed leasing.

for.name: Rep. Andrew Ireland
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill prohibiting offshore leasing off southwest Florida and recruited ten other Florida House members to join as original cosponsors.

for.name: 20 of 257 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including Florida members such as Dante Fascell and Bill Nelson.

for.name: 11 of 175 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including Florida members such as C.W. Young and Porter Goss.

against.name: House Interior and Insular Affairs Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired in the 101st Congress by Rep. George Miller
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to its Water, Power and Offshore Energy Resources Subcommittee on September 8, 1989, and never reported it out, so it never reached the House floor.

against.name: Oil and gas industry
against.role: Offshore drilling operators and leaseholders in the Gulf of Mexico
against.what_they_did: The industry generally opposed permanent drilling bans on federal offshore areas during this period, favoring lease sales in the eastern Gulf.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's support was bipartisan — 20 of 31 cosponsors were Democrats and 11 were Republicans, all or mostly Floridians — and there is no record of a floor vote for either party to oppose.

industries.note: The bill would have permanently closed the eastern Gulf off Florida to new federal leasing and blocked exploration and production approvals there, and required taxpayers to fund buybacks of existing leases. Florida's coastal economy depended on keeping that water unspoiled.

Keeping drilling out of the waters off southwest Florida and the Keys protects the beaches, fisheries, and marine environment that the state's tourism and seafood businesses depend on. The bill never became law, so these gains never materialized.
